notes.meaning: The Lord commanded Moses to set apart every firstborn male among Israel, whether human or animal, as His special property. To consecrate means to set something apart from ordinary everyday use for sacred service to God. Because the Lord had spared the firstborn of Israel when He struck down those of Egypt, He claimed them as uniquely His own.

Moses commanded the people never to forget the day they left their bitter slavery in Egypt. They were to remember that their freedom came by God's mighty power rather than their own strength. Eating bread made without yeast served as an ongoing reminder of that hasty departure.

Israel was leaving on this exact day in the spring month of Abib. The name Abib means green ears of grain, marking the season when the barley ripened and new plant life began. It was a pleasant spring season that God chose for their journey into the desert.

When the Lord brought Israel into the rich, fruitful land He had promised to their ancestors, they were to keep this same memorial service every year in that month. The phrase flowing with milk and honey described a fertile country full of pasture for livestock and flowers for bees. The celebration was not just for the moment of departure, but for all future generations in their new home.

For seven full days each year, the people were to eat unleavened bread, finishing with a special feast day to the Lord. During this whole week, no yeast was permitted in their homes or anywhere within their borders. This strict removal reminded them of how quickly they were rushed out of Egypt before their dough could rise.

Parents were told to teach their children during this feast why they observed these customs. They were to explain personally that this was done because of what the Lord did for them when bringing them out of slavery. Sharing God's great rescue keeps faith alive across generations.

Celebrating the feast was to serve as a constant reminder, as obvious as a sign tied to a person's hand or placed on their forehead. Its purpose was to keep the Lord's teaching on their lips and in their regular conversation. By practicing this memorial, Israel would always remember the mighty power God showed in delivering them.

God commanded Israel to keep this yearly festival at its designated time every year without fail. The Hebrew phrase means year after year as the seasons rolled by. It was an enduring statute intended to guide their worship down through history.

Once the Lord brought the Israelites into the land promised to their ancestors, they had to give every firstborn male to Him. This applied to human firstborn sons as well as the male offspring of their livestock. Setting them apart meant transferring ownership from the person so the animal or child belonged entirely to God.

An unclean animal like a donkey could not be sacrificed on an altar, so it had to be redeemed, or bought back, with an acceptable clean animal like a lamb. If an owner refused to buy back the donkey, its neck had to be broken so no one profited from it. Human sacrifice was strictly forbidden, so every firstborn son was also redeemed with a substitute payment.

When a child in later times asked why firstborn males were set apart, parents were to recount how Pharaoh refused to let Israel go. Because Pharaoh hardened his heart, the Lord struck down every firstborn in Egypt among people and cattle. Clean firstborn animals were offered in sacrifice to the Lord in gratitude, while firstborn human sons were redeemed through a ransom price.

This dedication of the firstborn served as another lasting sign on the hand and between the eyes. It kept the memory of God's miraculous rescue fresh in the nation's thoughts and daily actions. Remembering God's strong hand helps His people remain devoted to Him.

God did not lead the Israelites along the short coastal road through the land of the Philistines, even though it was the fastest route to Canaan. He knew the people were former slaves who were not yet spiritually or emotionally ready to face war. If they faced immediate conflict, they might panic, lose heart, and head back to Egypt.

Instead of the quick route, God led the people by a roundabout way through the wilderness toward the Red Sea. Although inexperienced, the Israelites marched out in orderly ranks rather than a chaotic mob. God wisely prepares His people by leading them along paths that teach them to rely entirely on Him.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars translate the phrase as 'Sea of Reeds' and understand it as a body of water located near the northern end of the Gulf of Suez rather than the open Red Sea.

notes.meaning: Moses carried the bones of Joseph out of Egypt to honor a solemn promise made centuries earlier. Joseph had trusted that God would one day visit Israel and lead them back to the Promised Land. Keeping Joseph's oath was a visible witness to his great faith in God's promises.

The Israelites traveled from their first stop at Succoth and set up camp at Etham on the edge of the desert. This outpost marked the border where the inhabited territory ended and the vast wilderness began. It was the starting point for their journey into the unknown barren land.

The Lord Himself guided the people openly, going before them in a pillar of cloud during the day and a pillar of fire at night. This provided a visible sign of God's presence that gave shade in the daytime heat and light in the dark. It allowed the large multitude to travel safely whenever God called them to move.

Neither the pillar of cloud by day nor the pillar of fire by night ever left the people throughout their wilderness journey. This constant symbol of God's presence remained faithfully with them until they reached the edge of the Promised Land. God never abandons His people when He leads them into difficult places.
